panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Patient 1 with Aarskog syndrome per caption and article title. Caption states distinctive facial characteristics and interdigital tracts in both hands; hands visibly short supporting brachydactyly. 6-year-old boy per in-text. B: Patient 2 captioned as Aarskog syndrome with shawl scrotum visible, classic genital manifestation. C: Patient 3 and mother patient 8 captioned with prominent forehead, widow's peak, hypertelorism, fold under lower lip, all classic Aarskog facial features. Mixed child and adult in same panel so age_group unknown. D: Patient 4 captioned with widow's peak, midface hypoplasia, ptosis, clinodactyly and brachydactyly, directly supporting vocabulary findings. E: Patient 5, brother of patient 4, captioned with distinctive facial features, clinodactyly and brachydactyly, classic Aarskog hand manifestations.

panels.figure_caption: Patients with clinical features of Aarskog syndrome. (A) Patient 1; note distinctive facial characteristics and interdigital tracts in both hands. (B) Patient 2; discrete facial features and the shawl scrotum can be appreciated. (C) Patient 3 and his mother (patient 8); note prominent forehead, widow's peak, hypertelorism, and fold under the lower lip. (D) Patient 4 with widow's peak, midface hypoplasia, ptosis, clinodactyly, and brachydactyly. (E) Patient 5, brother of patient 4, with distinctive facial features, clinodactyly, and brachydactyly.
in_text_mentions: the lower lip were observed in 100% of patients; brachydactyly, interdigital tracts, and shawl scrotum were also seen in 80% of patients. Secondary criteria included a widow's peak, present in 100% of patients, followed by cryptorchidism, dysplastic ears, and joint hypermobility in 80% of patients. Finally, among the additional features described, long philtrum and mid-facial hypoplasia were present in 80% of patients, followed by poor dental occlusion and frontal bossing, present in 60% of patients. Photographs of some patients with the observed clinical characteristics are shown in Figure1.

located within the FGD1 DH domain (Fig.2), which has been shown to play an important role in regulating cell growth and differentiation (Pasteris et al. 1994). Interestingly, the residue 380 was already detected as involved in mutational events, although the type of mutation is missense (p.E380A) (Orrico et al. 2004). This mutation was identified in the mother and child (patients 1 and 6). Patient 1, a 6-year-old boy evaluated due to short stature at 2 years of age, had eight primary, clinical criteria identified (Fig.1A), while his mother, patient 6, had attenuated features of this syndrome.
